questions.question_text:
Let $f(x)=\frac1{x-1}+3$.
State the domain and range of its inverse.

options.why: This retains the original domain and range instead of exchanging them.
This drops both exclusions: the inverse cannot take input $3$ or give output $1$.
This treats the excluded values $3$ and $1$ as inclusive lower bounds instead of excluding only those values.

questions.solution_text:
$D_f=\mathbb R\setminus\{1\}$
$R_f=\mathbb R\setminus\{3\}$
Exchange their roles.
$D=\mathbb R\setminus\{3\},\ R=\mathbb R\setminus\{1\}$

questions.question_text:
Let $f(x)=(x-2)^2+4,\ x\ge2$.
State the domain and range of $f^{-1}$.

options.why: This retains the original intervals instead of exchanging the domain and range.
This ignores the original minimum output $4$, which is the inverse's minimum input.
This ignores the original restriction $x\ge2$, which makes the inverse's outputs at least $2$.

questions.solution_text:
$D_f=[2,\infty),\ R_f=[4,\infty)$
Swap the domain and range.

questions.question_text:
Let $f(x)=(x-6)^2+3,\ x\le6$.
State the domain and range of $f^{-1}$.

options.why: This retains the original domain and range instead of exchanging them.
This uses the right-hand branch even though the original domain is $x\le6$.
This excludes the vertex values even though the original domain includes $x=6$.

questions.solution_text:
$D_f=(-\infty,6],\ R_f=[3,\infty)$
Swap the domain and range.
$D=[3,\infty),\ R=(-\infty,6]$

questions.question_text:
Let $f(x)=\sqrt{2x-6}+4$.
State the domain and range of $f^{-1}$.

options.why: This retains the original domain and range instead of exchanging them.
This ignores the added $4$, so it uses $0$ instead of $4$ as the original minimum output.
This uses $6$ as the original minimum input instead of dividing $2x\ge6$ by $2$ to obtain $x\ge3$.

questions.solution_text:
$2x-6\ge0$, so $D_f=[3,\infty)$.
The square root is non-negative, so $R_f=[4,\infty)$.
Swap the domain and range.
$D=[4,\infty),\ R=[3,\infty)$

questions.question_text:
Let $f(x)=\frac1{x-6}+8$.
State the domain and range of its inverse.

options.why: This retains the original exclusions instead of exchanging them: the inverse excludes input $8$ and output $6$.
This drops both exclusions: the inverse cannot take input $8$ or give output $6$.
This converts the excluded values $8$ and $6$ into inclusive lower bounds instead of excluding only those values.

questions.solution_text:
$D_f=\mathbb R\setminus\{6\}$
$R_f=\mathbb R\setminus\{8\}$
Exchange their roles.
$D=\mathbb R\setminus\{8\},\ R=\mathbb R\setminus\{6\}$

questions.question_text:
Let $f(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{x+7}}$.
State the domain and range of $f^{-1}$.

options.why: This includes output $-7$, but the original function is undefined at input $-7$ because its denominator is zero.
This retains the original domain and range instead of exchanging them.
This includes input $0$, but the original function approaches output $0$ without reaching it.

questions.solution_text:
The denominator must be real and non-zero, so $x+7>0$.
$D_f=(-7,\infty)$
The outputs are positive, approach $0$ without reaching it, and have no upper bound.
$R_f=(0,\infty)$
Swap the domain and range.
$D=(0,\infty),\ R=(-7,\infty)$

questions.question_text:
Let $f(x)=(x+2)^2-5,\ -5<x\le-2$.
State the domain and range of $f^{-1}$.

options.why: This includes the original excluded input $-5$ and its corresponding output $4$.
This retains the original domain and range instead of exchanging them.
This ignores the finite original lower bound $x>-5$ and uses the whole left-hand branch.

questions.solution_text:
$D_f=(-5,-2]$
On this domain, $(x+2)^2$ takes values in $[0,9)$, so $R_f=[-5,4)$.
Swap the domain and range, preserving the endpoints.
$D=[-5,4),\ R=(-5,-2]$
